name: Primary Lymphedema with Systemic or Visceral Involvement

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical Diagnostic Criteria for Primary Lymphedema with Systemic Involvement

criteria.description: Presence of chronic, non-pitting lymphedema primarily affecting lower limbs
Evidence of systemic or visceral lymphatic dysfunction (e.g., pleural effusion, ascites, or intestinal lymphangiectasia)
Positive family history of primary lymphedema or lymphatic disorders
Exclusion of secondary causes of lymphedema such as infection, malignancy, or surgery
Lymphoscintigraphy or MR lymphangiography demonstrating lymphatic hypoplasia or dysfunction

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of chronic primary lymphedema with documented systemic or visceral lymphatic involvement and exclusion of secondary causes
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing may aid diagnosis but is not mandatory.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Chronic non-pitting lymphedema of lower extremities
Visceral lymphatic dysfunction manifesting as chylous ascites
Pleural effusion due to lymphatic leakage

common.symptomName: Recurrent cellulitis or lymphangitis in affected limbs
Chronic fatigue related to protein loss and lymphatic dysfunction
searchTerms: chronic weakness due to lymph problems

common.symptomName: Cutaneous hyperkeratosis and papillomatosis over lymphedematous skin

occasional.symptomName: Chylothorax secondary to thoracic duct involvement
Lymphadenopathy in regional lymph node basins

laboratory: Hypoalbuminemia and hypogammaglobulinemia due to protein-losing enteropathy
Elevated lymphocyte count in pleural or ascitic fluid
Low total protein in chylous effusions
imaging: Lymphoscintigraphy showing lymphatic hypoplasia or obstruction
MR lymphangiography demonstrating abnormal lymphatic channels
Ultrasound or CT showing chylous ascites or pleural effusions
genetic: Mutations in genes related to lymphangiogenesis (e.g., FLT4, FOXC2) may be identified
other: Histopathology of affected skin showing dermal lymphatic dilation
Lymphatic vessel biopsy demonstrating hypoplasia or aplasia

distinguishingFeatures: History of infection, trauma, surgery, or malignancy
Absence of systemic or visceral lymphatic involvement
Later onset compared to primary forms
Congenital onset of lymphedema without systemic involvement
Lymphedema usually develops at puberty without visceral involvement

redFlags: Rapid progression of lymphedema with systemic symptoms
Development of chylous effusions causing respiratory compromise
Signs of protein-losing enteropathy with severe hypoalbuminemia
references: Orphanet: Primary lymphedema with systemic or visceral involvement, ORPHA:568044
